title: Better Call GPT: Comparing Large Language Models Against Lawyers
author: Lauren Martin · Nick Whitehouse · Stephanie Yiu · Lizzie Catterson · Rivindu Perera

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Legal benchmarks: Realistic tasks expose uneven competence
st.an: The source accepts task-specific, practice-oriented benchmarking and materially extends it through direct comparison with junior lawyers and LPOs on contract review, while adding time and cost as deployment-relevant measures. The supplied passage describes this design contribution but provides no results on comparative competence or reliability.
qs: By comparing the capabilities and efficiency of LLMs with those of human legal practitioners in the specific context of contract review, our study addresses a critical gap in the current research landscape.

Our study not only benchmarks the performance of LLMs against human practitioners but also evaluates their efficiency in terms of time and cost, offering valuable insights into the practical application of these models in legal settings.

st.t: Legal workflows: Immediate gains create competence risks
st.an: The study materially extends the cluster with direct experimental evidence that advanced LLMs can match or exceed human accuracy while delivering major speed and cost gains in a bounded contract-review task. It also supports workflow reconfiguration and entry-level pressure rather than wholesale lawyer replacement, while appropriately limiting generalisation and acknowledging reliability risks. Its stronger disruption predictions go beyond the evidence but do not displace its overall alignment.
qs: Our empirical analysis benchmarks LLMs against a ground truth set by Senior Lawyers, uncovering that advanced models match or exceed human accuracy in determining legal issues.

While our research does not explore a broad enough spectrum of the capabilities performed by Junior Lawyers to establish a one to one comparison, it does indicate that LLMs are already outperforming Junior Lawyers in specific areas.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s task-specific, human-supervised framing and materially extends it with a direct contract-review comparison showing strong issue-determination, speed and cost performance alongside weaker, model-dependent issue localisation. It also links those uneven capabilities to workflow redesign and predicted changes in junior-lawyer and LPO work, while expressly limiting broader substitution claims.
qs: However, a LLMs ability to locate issues within contracts, particularly where a standard is  not present, is model-dependent and may not consistently outperform human practitioners, highlighting the importance of selecting the right model for the legal task.

While our research does not explore a broad enough spectrum of the capabilities performed by Junior Lawyers to establish a one to one comparison, it does indicate that LLMs are already outperforming Junior Lawyers in specific areas.

st.t: Benchmark success: Average scores conceal complete-task failure
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s distinction between strong benchmark averages and dependable end-to-end legal work. It finds near-human performance on issue determination but materially weaker issue-location performance that constrains autonomous contract markup. Its broader claim of LLM dominance overreaches these task-specific results but does not outweigh the study’s explicit qualification.
qs: Arguably, the lower performance by LLMs in locating issues could impact their ability to accurately mark up contracts on their own, constraining their effectiveness in eliminating the role of a Lawyer in contract review.

kp.k: Ten-contract experiment benchmarks review against senior-lawyer consensus
kp.d: This 2024 working paper, conducted by Onit’s AI Center of Excellence, compares six LLMs with junior lawyers and legal process outsourcers (LPOs) on determining and locating legal issues. The dataset contains ten anonymised procurement contracts balanced between US and New Zealand jurisdictions and supplier and buyer perspectives. Reviews use document scenarios and a standardised playbook; senior-lawyer majority consensus supplies the benchmark. NDAs were excluded as insufficiently complex for the intended evaluation.
qs: Data for this study were collected from ten procurement contracts, sourced from real-world legal agreements and anonymised to preserve confidentiality.

This collected data was then aggregated to formulate benchmarks for each evaluative criterion, relying on the majority consensus to determine both compliance with the standard and the precise location of the relevant contractual reference.

kp.k: Model selection favours whole-contract context over retrieval
kp.d: The study selected GPT4 32k, GPT4-1106, GPT3.5-turbo-16k, Claude 2.1, Claude 2.0 and Palm2 Text-bison-32k-2, all at temperature 0.2. Models supporting fewer than 16,000 tokens were excluded. The authors report that splitting contracts required repeated contextual material and that preliminary RAG approaches introduced contextual discontinuities. Model-specific prompts combined a lawyer persona, review task, contract scenario and checklist.
qs: models that could not support at least 16,000 tokens were considered inadequate for our purposes and were subsequently excluded from our analysis.
The RAG approach, in particular, was found to introduce discontinuities in the contextual understanding of the contracts.
Prompts were structured with the following elements; the role, the task and the context.

kp.k: Human benchmark includes variation among senior lawyers
kp.d: The authors use Cronbach’s Alpha to report agreement: 0.923366 across all participants, 0.719308 among senior lawyers, 0.765058 among juniors and 1 among LPO practitioners. They interpret the lower senior-lawyer value as suggesting more varied approaches to issue identification and speculate that juniors’ greater agreement may reflect consistent training or adherence to established frameworks.
qs: The overall agreement among all participants was remarkably high, with an Alpha value of 0.923366, indicating a very strong consensus.
Interestingly, the agreement among Senior Lawyers alone was the lowest at 0.719308, suggesting a more varied approach to issue identification in contracts among experience practitioners.
Notably, the agreement among LPO practitioners reached a perfect Alpha of 1, indicating absolute uniformity in their responses.

kp.k: GPT4-1106 nearly matches LPOs in issue determination
kp.d: Table 2 reports issue-determination F-scores of 0.874 for LPOs, 0.871 for GPT4-1106 and 0.860 for juniors. GPT4-32k scores 0.820, Claude 2.0 scores 0.817, Claude 2.1 scores 0.809, Palm2 text-bison scores 0.708 and GPT3.5 scores 0.657. Precision and recall differ: GPT4-1106 records 0.835 precision and 0.910 recall, against LPOs’ 0.933 and 0.823. The authors describe the leading model as on par with LPOs and slightly ahead of juniors on this task.
qs: In the issue determination aspect, both GPT4-1106 and LPO practitioners emerged as the top performers with an F-score of 0.87, indicating a high level of precision and reliability in this aspect.
Junior lawyers achieved an F-score of 0.86 suggesting that their expertise is slightly below the leading LLMs in determining legal issues.

kp.k: Locating issues remains harder and model-dependent
kp.d: Table 3 gives LPOs the highest issue-location F-score, 0.770, followed by GPT4-32k at 0.740, Claude 2.1 at 0.701, GPT4-1106 at 0.686, juniors at 0.667, Claude 2.0 at 0.631, GPT3.5 at 0.620 and Palm2 text-bison at 0.452. The authors acknowledge that localisation limitations could constrain autonomous contract markup, particularly where required provisions are absent. Nevertheless, they characterise the 0.03 gap between the best model and LPOs as trivial and assert equivalent review quality; that equivalence is their interpretation.
qs: However, a LLMs ability to locate issues within contracts, particularly where a standard is not present, is model-dependent and may not consistently outperform human practitioners, highlighting the importance of selecting the right model for the legal task.

Arguably, the lower performance by LLMs in locating issues could impact their ability to accurately mark up contracts on their own, constraining their effectiveness in eliminating the role of a Lawyer in contract review.
we believe the 0.03 F-score difference between LPOs and LLMs is trivial

kp.k: Review processing times substantially favour LLMs
kp.d: Table 4 reports average minutes per document of 43.46 for seniors, 56.17 for juniors and 201.00 for LPOs, versus 4.70 for GPT4-1106, 2.11 for GPT4-32k, 1.44 for GPT3.5, 2.05 for Claude 2.1, 1.63 for Claude 2.0 and 0.73 for Palm2 text-bison. Section 5.2 gives the fastest model’s time as 0.728 minutes and describes it as 276 times faster than LPOs and 77 times faster than juniors. The authors additionally argue that concurrent requests enable greater throughput.
qs: Amongst the human practitioners, Senior Lawyers demonstrated the most efficiency averaging 43.46 minutes per document, while Junior Lawyers took slightly longer, averaging 56.17 minutes.
For instance, the fastest LLM outpaces LPOs by an astonishing 276-fold and Junior Lawyers by 77-fold.
Moreover, LLMs possess the capacity to handle multiple requests concurrently, exponentially increasing the volume of contracts they can assess.

kp.k: Prompt preparation reportedly parallels human instruction time
kp.d: The authors report an average 16 hours spent setting up, testing, fine-tuning and validating system prompts. They say this matches the time devoted to instructing junior lawyers and LPOs on comparable tasks, arguing that preparation does not offset the models’ operational speed advantage.
qs: Our research found that setting up, testing, fine-tuning, and validating the LLMs’ system prompts took an average of 16 hours.
Notably, this investment is on par with the time dedicated to instructing Junior Lawyers and LPOs for similar tasks.

kp.k: Reported direct review costs fall dramatically
kp.d: Human costs combine average review time with hourly rates derived from compensation benchmarks and Onit market data; model costs use commercial token or character pricing. Table 5 reports USD per document of $75.92 for seniors, $74.26 for juniors, $36.85 for LPOs, $0.25 for GPT4-1106, $1.24 for GPT4-32k, $0.05 for GPT3.5, $0.02 for each Claude model and $0.03 for Palm2 text-bison. Section 5.3 instead describes the fastest model as costing approximately two cents and claims reductions exceeding 99.97 percent against juniors and 99.94 percent against LPOs.
qs: The cost per contract for human practitioners was calculated based on their average time spent on a contact and their respective hourly rates.

For LLMs, the cost was determined by the average number of input and output tokens, and the respective cost per token, except for Palm2 text-bison which was priced based on the number of characters used.
This equates to a cost reduction of more than 99.97 percent when compared to Junior Lawyers, and 99.94 percent compared to LPOs.

kp.k: Semantic errors and supervision qualify automation claims
kp.d: The appendix attributes a significant portion of LLM inaccuracies to misinterpreting wording and missing legal nuances, contrasting this with senior lawyers’ sensitivity to semantic differences. The discussion explicitly conditions the optimistic scaling outlook on review quality and ongoing supervision of outputs. These qualifications accompany, rather than disappear behind, the paper’s broader claim that LLMs are superior review tools.
qs: This phenomenon was especially pronounced in the LLMs, where a significant portion of inaccuracies was linked to the misinterpretation of specific wordings.

In comparison, the Senior Lawyers, serving as the benchmark for this study, showed exceptional care in interpreting subtle differences in language, indicating a sophisticated understanding of semantic variations.
Nevertheless, this optimistic outlook should be tempered with careful consideration of the quality of reviews and the need for ongoing supervision of LLM outputs.

kp.k: LPOs predicted to shift toward operating AI
kp.d: The authors predict substantial disruption to LPOs from models’ combined accuracy, speed and cost advantages. They suggest providers may move from manual legal processes toward managing LLM technology, quality control, interpretation and nuanced application of outputs. This is a prospective business-model argument, not an observed provider transition in the experiment.
qs: We believe LLMs are already at a point where they can significantly disrupt LPOs.

There is little doubt that broad adoption of LLMs will lead to a significant shift in the LPO business model, necessitating a need for LPOs to pivot from providing manual legal process services, perhaps to becoming managers and operators of LLM technology, focusing on quality control, interpretation, and nuanced application of the insights generated by these models.

kp.k: Junior employment and career progression may change
kp.d: The authors predict that partial LLM adoption will reduce demand for entry-level positions as currently defined over time, while established juniors undertake complex, high-value work earlier. They expressly acknowledge that the experiment does not cover enough junior-lawyer capabilities to establish a one-to-one comparison. No quantified employment effect or specific timetable is supplied.
qs: While our research does not explore a broad enough spectrum of the capabilities performed by Junior Lawyers to establish a one to one comparison, it does indicate that LLMs are already outperforming Junior Lawyers in specific areas.
We believe the partial adoption of LLMs will begin to reduce the demand for entry-level legal positions, as they are currently defined, over time.
In contrast, established Junior Lawyers will engage in more complex, high-value work earlier in their careers, as routine tasks are gradually transitioned to LLMs.

kp.k: Authors predict competition, scalability and broader accessibility
kp.d: The authors anticipate law firms and legal departments increasing review throughput without proportional cost increases and early adopters gaining a competitive edge. They predict an adoption arms race and speculate that resistance may protect established interests rather than reflect technological or ethical concerns. Their claims about accessibility, access to justice and public trust are projected implications, not outcomes measured by the contract-review experiment.
qs: The adoption of LLMs will enable legal departments and law firms to substantially increase their contract review throughput without a proportional increase in costs.
Early adopters of this technology are poised to gain a significant competitive edge, likely triggering an arms race in the legal sector.
genuine resistance to LLM adoption may be less about the validity of the technology—as evidenced by our research—and more about protecting established interests.

kp.k: Broader contracts and negotiation require further research
kp.d: The authors call for a larger ground-truth dataset and evaluation across more contract types. They identify contract negotiation as a further research area requiring contextual understanding beyond contract text. These recommendations delimit the study’s demonstrated task coverage despite its expansive conclusions about legal-industry transformation.
qs: To build on our findings, further research is needed to evaluate LLM performance across a broader range of contract types and to expand the ground truth dataset.
Additionally, we are interested in exploring LLMs’ capabilities in contract negotiation—a complex area requiring contextual understanding beyond the contract text itself.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Martin and co-authors claim that leading LLMs already match junior lawyers and LPOs in determining contractual legal issues, although issue-location performance is model-dependent.
pts.d: The authors report GPT4-1106's issue-determination F-score as 0.871, compared with 0.874 for LPOs and 0.860 for junior lawyers. For locating issues, LPOs score 0.770, the leading model GPT4-32k scores 0.740, and junior lawyers score 0.667. The authors regard the 0.03 location-score gap as trivial and assert LPO-level review quality, while acknowledging that localization shortcomings could constrain autonomous contract markup and lawyer substitution.

pts.k: The authors claim major speed and direct-cost advantages that could increase contract-review throughput and scalability.
pts.d: The paper reports model processing times of 0.73–4.70 minutes per document, versus 56.17 minutes for junior lawyers and 201 minutes for LPOs. It describes the fastest model as 276 times faster than LPOs and 77 times faster than junior lawyers. Table 5 reports model costs of $0.02–$1.24 per document, versus $74.26 for juniors and $36.85 for LPOs. Section 5.3 claims reductions of more than 99.97 percent relative to juniors and 99.94 percent relative to LPOs. Its approximately two-cent illustration differs from Table 5's three-cent cost for the fastest model, Palm2. The authors extrapolate from these task-level comparisons to higher organizational throughput and concurrent review capacity.

pts.k: The authors predict disruption of LPO business models and declining demand for entry-level legal roles as currently defined.
pts.d: They argue that LLMs are already capable of disrupting manual outsourced legal-process services. Under broad adoption, LPOs may shift toward operating models, quality control, interpretation and nuanced application. They separately predict that partial adoption will reduce entry-level demand over time and move established junior lawyers into complex, high-value work earlier. These are market and workforce predictions drawn from the contract-review findings, rather than employment outcomes measured by the experiment.

pts.k: The authors predict competitive advantages for early adopters and potentially wider access to legal services.
pts.d: They anticipate an adoption race among legal organizations, and suggest lower-cost scalability could make services available to more users or clients. They also speculate that resistance may reflect protection of established interests rather than technological or ethical concerns, potentially affecting trust and access to justice. These broader competitive and public-access consequences are not directly measured in the contract experiment; the accessibility argument is framed as a possibility.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The accuracy claims rest on an Onit-conducted comparison of six models and human reviewers against senior-lawyer consensus on ten procurement contracts.
pts.d: The authors, affiliated with Onit's AI Center of Excellence, use anonymized real-world US and New Zealand procurement contracts, contextual scenarios and a standardized review playbook, balanced between buyer and supplier perspectives. Senior-lawyer majority consensus establishes issue-determination and issue-location ground truth. Tables 2 and 3 report precision, recall and F-scores. This is the authors' own task-specific benchmark, distinct from LegalBench, which appears in related work. The appendix supplies examples of missed written-notice and written-consent requirements as evidence of limitations in interpreting legal wording.

pts.k: Efficiency claims use measured review durations, benchmarked lawyer rates and commercial model pricing; disruption predictions extrapolate from those comparisons.
pts.d: Human per-contract costs are calculated from average review time and hourly rates, drawing on the ACC's 2023 compensation survey and Onit-held market data. Model costs use input/output token pricing or character pricing for Palm2. The authors report an average 16-hour investment in setting up, testing, fine-tuning and validating system prompts, which they say is comparable to instructing human reviewers. The reported per-document cost method is a processing-cost comparison, not a separately reported costing of ongoing human verification. No longitudinal adoption, employment, competition or unmet legal-need data are offered for the broader predictions.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The paper presents task-level capability and LPO disruption potential as current in 2024; wider organizational and employment changes depend on adoption and unfold without a specified deadline.
pts.d: The experiment concerns selected GPT-4, GPT-3.5, Claude 2 and Palm2 versions, using model-specific prompts, temperature 0.2 and context windows of at least 16,000 tokens. Claims apply to playbook-based issue determination and location in procurement contracts, not a tested full range of legal practice. The authors explicitly qualify junior-lawyer comparisons, call for broader contract datasets and leave negotiation to future work. They acknowledge ongoing supervision and review quality as conditions on the optimistic cost and scalability outlook. Broad adoption is the condition for the predicted LPO business-model shift; even partial adoption is predicted to affect entry-level demand over time.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The principal affected groups are outsourced legal-process providers, junior lawyers, corporate legal departments, law firms and prospective service users.
pts.d: The immediate task segment is high-volume procurement-contract review ordinarily delegated to juniors or outsourced practitioners. LPOs face possible substitution of manual work and a transition into AI operation and quality control. Junior lawyers face reduced demand for routine entry-level work but earlier exposure to more complex assignments. Corporate legal departments are buyer-side beneficiaries of efficiency, while law firms are provider-side beneficiaries and competitors in the predicted adoption race. Senior lawyers supply the study's benchmark; the experiment does not establish replacement of their broader expertise. Potential benefits for wider client populations and access to justice are projected rather than demonstrated through measurement of unmet civil legal need.
